question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete straight into the blood
options.B: Endocrine glands release sweat and digestive enzymes onto body surfaces
options.C: Exocrine glands use rich capillary networks instead of tubular ducts
options.D: Exocrine glands produce chemical messengers for distant target organs

explanation: Think of endocrine glands as being ductless—they pour their chemical messages directly into the bloodstream. Exocrine glands, like sweat glands, use tubes (ducts) to send their products to a body surface. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in the body?

options.A: Filtering metabolic waste products out of circulating blood plasma
options.B: Directing immediate, split-second muscle movements and reflexes
options.C: Coordinating slow, sustained processes like growth and metabolism
options.D: Producing physical barriers to protect internal organs from pathogens

explanation: While your nervous system handles quick reflexes (like pulling your hand from a hot stove), the endocrine system takes the long view—slowly and steadily managing things like your growth, mood, and metabolism. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which group of hormones is made directly from cholesterol?
explanation: Steroid hormones are built using cholesterol as their base material. Because of this, they share a fat-loving (lipophilic) nature! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why do steroid hormones need carrier proteins to travel through the blood?

options.A: Because carrier proteins protect them from being digested by blood enzymes
options.B: Because they are fat-soluble and do not dissolve well in water-based blood plasma
options.C: Because they are too large to fit through the walls of blood capillaries alone
options.D: Because carrier proteins are required to activate their chemical structure

explanation: Since blood is mostly water and steroid hormones are fat-based, they don't mix well on their own. Carrier proteins act like VIP transport vehicles to get them safely through the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the very first, inactive protein chain made from mRNA during peptide hormone production called?
explanation: Before a peptide hormone is ready, the cell makes a starter version called a preprohormone. It gets trimmed down step-by-step into the active hormone! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: Where does a prohormone usually get turned into its final, active hormone form?

options.A: Inside secretory vesicles as they wait to be released
options.B: Directly on the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
options.C: Inside the cell nucleus during the transcription of DNA
options.D: Out in the bloodstream after the molecule leaves the cell

explanation: The final cutting and polishing happens right inside the storage bubbles (secretory vesicles) as the cell waits for the signal to release the hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which parts of the cell contain the tools needed to turn cholesterol into steroid hormones?

options.B: Lysosomes and the cell plasma membrane
options.D: The cell nucleus and the Golgi apparatus

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! The mitochondria and the smooth endoplasmic reticulum team up to convert cholesterol into active steroid hormones. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why can steroid hormones slip right out of cells as soon as they are made?

options.A: They are pushed out by water pressure inside the cytoplasm
options.B: They are small enough to pass through active transport protein pumps
options.C: They are stored in large vesicles that burst open upon stimulation
options.D: They are fat-soluble and can cross lipid cell membranes easily

explanation: Because cell membranes are also made of fats (lipids), fat-loving steroid hormones pass straight through them like an open door—no special channels needed! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: How do cells release stored peptide hormones into the fluid outside the cell?
explanation: Peptide hormones are packed in little bubbles that fuse with the cell membrane, popping open to spill their contents outside. That process is called exocytosis! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: What must a cell do if it makes steroid hormones and suddenly receives a continuous call to release more?

options.A: It must rapidly synthesize new hormone molecules from cholesterol on the spot
options.B: It pumps stored hormones out of the cytoplasm using ATP energy channels
options.C: It opens storage vesicle gates to release a large backup supply of ready hormones
options.D: It stops producing hormones until old supplies are cleared from the blood

explanation: Unlike peptide hormones, steroid hormones aren't stored in large stockpiles. If the body needs more right now, the cell has to manufacture them fresh from cholesterol immediately. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the body's main way of stopping hormone levels from climbing too high?
explanation: Negative feedback is like a thermostat: when hormone levels get too high, a signal is sent to slow down production and bring things back to normal. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Insulin lowering blood glucose levels after a carbohydrate-rich meal
options.B: Cortisol suppressing the hypothalamus from releasing stress hormones
options.C: Oxytocin release intensifying uterine contractions during childbirth
options.D: Thyroid hormone stopping the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone

explanation: Positive feedback pushes a process even faster until the goal is met! Childbirth is a great example: oxytocin causes contractions, which trigger more oxytocin, until the baby is born. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: What term is used for the time it takes for half of a hormone to be cleared from the bloodstream?
explanation: Just like medicine in the body, a hormone's 'half-life' is simply how long it takes for half of its concentration in the blood to disappear. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: Which two organs do the heaviest lifting when it comes to breaking down and removing hormones?
explanation: Your liver chemically alters and breaks down used hormones, while your kidneys filter the leftovers out into your urine. Great tag-team work! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: What word describes an endocrine gland producing way too much hormone?
explanation: Break it down: 'hyper' means high or excessive, and 'secretion' means releasing a substance. So, hypersecretion means too much hormone output! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)

question: A patient has an autoimmune condition where their insulin-making cells are destroyed. What lab finding is most likely?

options.A: Dangerously low blood sugar caused by excess hormone release
options.B: Rapid weight gain due to slowed metabolic breakdown
options.C: Elevated blood glucose levels due to a lack of insulin
options.D: Increased water retention and high blood pressure

explanation: Without insulin (hyposecretion), glucose can't easily enter the body's cells to be used for energy. Instead, it builds up in the bloodstream, leading to high blood sugar. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)
